question: Capgemini Exceller technical interview. The candidate was tested on web basics: **describe the structure of an HTML document** (tags such as `html`, `head`, `body`, `div`), and **define inline, internal and external CSS** and how they differ.
lookingFor: Knows the skeleton of an HTML5 page and what each part is for.
Understands the three ways to apply CSS and their trade-offs.
Knows specificity and cascade order at a basic level.
Can speak about maintainability and performance, not just definitions.
answer:
**HTML document structure.** ```text metadata: meta charset, meta viewport, title, link to CSS visible content: header, main (with div blocks), footer, script tags ``` (each opening tag is paired with a matching closing tag in real markup) - `` tells the browser to use standards mode. - `` is the root element. - `` holds metadata that is not displayed: charset, viewport, title, links to CSS, and so on. - `` holds everything visible. Semantic tags (`header`, `nav`, `main`, `section`, `footer`) are preferred over many `div`s for accessibility and SEO; `div` is a generic block container. **Three ways to apply CSS.** - **Inline:** the `style` attribute on one element, e.g. `

`. Highest priority among normal rules, but it mixes content with style, cannot be reused and is hard to maintain. - **Internal:** a `style` block inside `head`. Applies to that page only. Fine for a single page or a quick demo. - **External:** a separate `.css` file linked with `link`. Best practice: one file styles many pages, the browser caches it, and the code stays maintainable. **Cascade.** When rules conflict, the browser considers importance (`!important`), then specificity (inline beats id beats class beats element), then source order (the later rule wins). Inline styles win on specificity, which is also why they make overriding painful. **Summary line.** Use external CSS for almost everything, internal for page-specific tweaks, inline only for dynamic values or email HTML.
